item.title: AI malware can rewrite itself to evade detection
item.description: Google's Threat Intelligence Group found PROMPTFLUX malware that uses Gemini to rewrite its own code every hour, raising urgent cybersecurity alarms.
item.content:encoded:
Google's Threat Intelligence Group found experimental malware called PROMPTFLUX that could ask Gemini to rewrite its own code. One version was designed to do that every hour. Why would malware keep rewriting itself? To make it harder to recognize.

Security software can look for known patterns in malicious code. If that code keeps changing, the malware becomes a moving target. That does not automatically make it invisible to current security tools, but it can make some types of detection more difficult.

There is an important reality check here. PROMPTFLUX was still being developed when Google found it. Researchers had yet to see it successfully compromise a victim's device or network, and Google disabled assets connected to the activity.

What caught my attention is what came next. Google has since documented AI being used by malware during live attacks. It has also uncovered an Android backdoor that can use AI to understand what is happening on a phone and help decide what to do next. That tells us where this could be heading. So let’s break down how AI-powered malware works and what you can do to protect yourself.

AN AI CYBERATTACK COULD TURN OFF AMERICA'S LIGHTS BEFORE WASHINGTON EVEN UNDERSTANDS WHY

NEW! 🩺 Free CyberGuy LIVE class: Get Better Healthcare With AI Saturday, September 26 at 11 a.m. ET / 8 a.m. PT

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will show you five practical ways AI can help you organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare smarter questions for your doctor. No technical experience is needed.

Save your free spot at CyberGuyLive.com

PROMPTFLUX was a VBScript-based malware project that Google discovered in June 2025. Its most interesting component was called the "Thinking Robot." The malware could contact Gemini and request new obfuscation techniques designed to make its code harder for security software to recognize.

Google later found multiple PROMPTFLUX variations. One included instructions telling Gemini to rewrite the malware’s entire source code every hour while preserving the pieces needed for it to continue working. Think about what that means from the defender’s side. Security software may identify one version of malicious code. Then the program can generate a different-looking version while continuing to pursue the same goal. That creates a moving target.

Google described PROMPTFLUX as an early example of "just-in-time" AI being built directly into malware. Instead of relying entirely on functions written ahead of time, malware can ask an AI model for help while it runs.

No, and this is where I want to be careful. You may hear AI malware described as something that can simply change its appearance and walk right past antivirus protection. The reality has more layers. Signature detection still plays a role in cybersecurity. Security software can recognize the digital fingerprints of known malware and block them quickly.

However, antivirus protection does much more than compare a file with a list of known threats. Microsoft Defender Antivirus, for example, uses real-time monitoring, behavioral analysis and heuristic protection. It also uses cloud-delivered protection and machine learning to help identify new threats that may not match a known malware signature.

That means changing the code does not automatically make malware invisible. A security tool may still notice suspicious behavior once the malware starts doing something dangerous. PROMPTFLUX is concerning because it can make one form of detection harder. That does not mean every layer of modern antivirus suddenly stops working.

PROMPTFLUX was experimental. PROMPTSTEAL crossed an important line. Google identified the Russian government-backed group APT28 using PROMPTSTEAL against targets in Ukraine. Google says this was its first observation of malware querying a large language model while deployed in live operations.

PROMPTSTEAL takes a different approach from PROMPTFLUX. Instead of asking AI to rewrite itself, it queries the Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct model through Hugging Face. The model generates Windows commands that PROMPTSTEAL can execute.

Those commands can gather information about a computer and copy documents from folders including Documents, Downloads and Desktop. The malware then sends collected information back to infrastructure controlled by the attacker. That is a significant change. The AI model becomes part of what the malware does after it starts running.

Then came PROMPTSPY. Google detailed the Android backdoor in May 2026 after it was initially identified by ESET. PROMPTSPY contains an AI-powered module called GeminiAutomationAgent. It can send information about what appears on an infected Android device to Gemini and use the response to help navigate the phone’s interface.

In other words, the malware can use AI to understand part of what is happening on the screen and determine how to interact with it. Google found that PROMPTSPY could also make itself harder to remove. When a victim tried to uninstall it, the malware could place an invisible overlay over the uninstall button so taps would appear to do nothing. There is some good news for Android users.

Google says it took action against the actor behind the malware. It also said no apps containing PROMPTSPY were found on Google Play at the time of its May report. Known versions are detected by Google Play Protect, which is enabled by default on Android devices with Google Play Services. Still, PROMPTSPY gives us a much clearer picture of where this technology could go. Malware can begin reacting to the device it finds instead of relying only on instructions written before the attack starts.

HALLUSQUATTING AI ATTACK COULD HIJACK YOUR COMPUTER

Google’s newest report makes the larger trend harder to ignore. On Sept. 8, 2026, Google Threat Intelligence Group said it had seen attackers move from basic AI prompting toward agentic AI workflows and AI-enabled automation. That means AI can start taking on larger pieces of an operation with less human involvement.

One example really jumped out at me. Google says a suspected financially motivated attacker compromised a company’s cloud infrastructure. The attacker then used an AI coding chatbot and agent instructions to plan, build and execute a mass credential-harvesting campaign in less than six hours. The system could manage vulnerability scanning and troubleshoot problems while the attack was underway. Google says thousands of third-party credentials were compromised.

Google has also seen attackers experimenting with automated reconnaissance and frameworks designed to manage harvested credentials. However, there is another important reality check. Google says it has yet to observe threat actors deploying fully autonomous exploit pipelines against targets in the wild. We have not reached the point where an AI system independently launches every part of a cyberattack without people involved. The amount of work AI can take off an attacker’s hands keeps growing, though.

AI arrives on top of an already huge malware problem. Independent security institute AV-TEST says it registers more than 450,000 new malicious programs and potentially unwanted applications every day. That number does not mean 450,000 completely different attacks are hitting people every day. Malware samples can include different versions and variations of existing threats.

Still, the volume shows why security companies cannot depend on recognizing every malicious file by its appearance alone. Meanwhile, the financial damage tied to cyber-enabled crime continues to climb. The FBI says Americans reported nearly $21 billion in cyber-enabled crime losses during 2025, up 26% from the year before. Those losses cover many kinds of online crime and cannot be attributed to AI malware. However, they show what criminals already stand to gain when technology makes attacks easier to run.

You do not need to understand how an AI model rewrites VBScript to protect yourself. The best defense still comes from making it harder for malware to reach your device and harder for it to succeed if something slips through.

Look for strong antivirus software with real-time protection and behavioral detection. That becomes especially useful when malicious software changes enough that a traditional signature may not recognize it immediately. The right protection can watch what a program does after it starts running. Suspicious file changes or attempts to alter sensitive system settings can trigger another layer of detection. If you are comparing protection, see our guide to what to look for in antivirus software without the jargon. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.

Security software cannot help as much if its strongest protections have been disabled. On Windows, Microsoft says Defender’s behavior monitoring is enabled by default. Cloud-delivered protection also helps detect new and emerging threats. If a website, pop-up or random tutorial tells you to disable antivirus protection so something will install, stop. Do not turn off security protections to make a questionable download work.

Keep your operating system and browser current. Do the same for software you use regularly. Attackers often look for people running software with vulnerabilities that already have patches available. Automatic updates can close those openings without forcing you to track every security bulletin yourself.

CHINA-LINKED HACKERS INFILTRATED US GOVERNMENT NETWORKS BEFORE FBI TAKEDOWN

This has become one of the most important malware warnings I can give you. Attackers increasingly use fake CAPTCHA pages and bogus error messages to tell victims to open Windows Run, PowerShell, Command Prompt or Terminal. The page then asks them to paste a command. Do not do it. A legitimate CAPTCHA should never require you to run a command on your computer. We recently reported that more than 5,400 compromised websites were being used in one campaign built around this trick. See how thousands of hacked sites can trick you into installing malware.

Security warnings can feel annoying when you are trying to download something quickly. Do not automatically click past them. Microsoft Defender SmartScreen, for example, can check websites and downloads for signs of phishing or malicious software. If your browser blocks a file or tells you a site looks dangerous, investigate before continuing. A website should never pressure you to weaken your computer’s security so you can proceed.

PROMPTSPY gives Android users a good reason to pay attention to where apps come from. Google says Play Protect checks apps for harmful behavior. It also scans apps installed from outside Google Play. Keep Play Protect enabled. Be especially cautious with sideloaded apps from websites, messages or unfamiliar app stores. The same thinking applies to browser extensions. An extension can gain significant access to what happens inside your browser, so install only what you need from a source you trust.

A password manager helps you create unique passwords for your accounts. It can also give you a useful phishing warning. If a saved password normally fills automatically and suddenly does not, stop and check the website address before typing the password yourself. Use multifactor authentication where available. Better yet, use a passkey when a service supports one. Keep in mind that some information-stealing malware can target browser cookies or authenticated sessions. MFA still helps, but no login protection gives you permission to ignore malware on the device itself.

Back up anything you would hate to lose. That could include family photos and financial records. Keep other irreplaceable files covered too. A cloud backup can help. An external drive that you disconnect when you are finished backing up can give you another recovery option. A backup will not stop malware from stealing data, but it can make ransomware or destructive malware much less devastating.

Watch for unfamiliar programs and unexplained security alerts. Pay attention if your antivirus suddenly turns itself off or your browser starts behaving strangely. If you think a computer may be infected, disconnect it from the internet and run a trusted security scan. For a PC, you can follow our guide on what to do if you think your PC has a virus. If passwords or financial information may have been exposed, use a different trusted device to change important passwords. Then sign out of active sessions where the service allows it. Check your financial accounts for activity you do not recognize. Act quickly if something looks wrong.

PROMPTFLUX caught my attention because of what it says about the direction malware is taking. For years, attackers have found ways to change malicious code and make detection harder. AI gives them another tool for doing that while the malware is running. I would not take that to mean antivirus protection suddenly became obsolete. Strong security software already looks beyond a simple malware fingerprint. Behavior monitoring and cloud-based analysis can help catch threats that have never been seen before. What concerns me more is how quickly the technology is progressing. PROMPTFLUX was experimental. PROMPTSTEAL appeared in live operations. PROMPTSPY showed how AI could help malware interpret an Android interface. Now Google is seeing attackers use agentic AI to automate larger portions of an attack. For me, the lesson is pretty straightforward. Do not depend on one security feature to save you. Keep good protection running, take security warnings seriously and make it difficult for malicious software to get onto your devices in the first place. If something does get through, reacting quickly can limit how far the damage goes.

As malware becomes capable of changing its code and making more decisions with AI, do you think security companies can stay ahead, or are we heading toward a point where it becomes much harder to know whether our devices are truly safe? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

item.title: 5 tough questions Colin Kaepernick didn't hear during his media tour | Matt Calkins
item.description: Colin Kaepernick sat down with "The View" and Trevor Noah to promote "The Perilous Fight," but not one interviewer challenged his boldest claims.
item.content:encoded:
There was "The View," "The Daily Show" and "The Pivot."

There was a sit-down with Trevor Noah and a chat with Jemele Hill.

Colin Kaepernick's face has been ubiquitous over the past few days as he's been promoting his new book "The Perilous Fight." But one thing has been conspicuously absent from the former NFL quarterback's press tour: a single probing question.

I get that Kaepernick wants to avoid tension while hyping up his memoir. He isn't going to choose an interviewer he thinks might give him pushback.

But it's been hard as a journalist to watch the wall-to-wall coddling of one of the most controversial figures of the past decade. To me, the story has become what's not being asked.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Some examples.

OutKick’s Bobby Burack noted the absurdity of the slave-trade comparison Kaepernick made during an interview with former ESPN analyst Ryan Clark. He said that he can draw a "parallel" between the combine and a slave auction because people are telling players to "strip down to your drawers."

Never mind that the NFL is completely voluntary and has produced more Black millionaires than any other business in the country. To Kaepernick, it's on par with one of history's most brutal systems of human exploitation.

Dumb? Yes. But what's dumber is that Kaepernick also said he's been training every morning in case an NFL team gives him a call. In other words — this league reminds him of a horrifying institution ... and he can't wait to get back.

Kaepernick's supporters will tell you that his protesting was peaceful. But he played a prominent role in the vilification of police that swept the country in the middle of last decade and again in 2020. The man wore pig socks. He compared police officers to modern-day "slave patrols." And it's this type of rhetoric that scared myriad police officers off the streets and led to a soaring Black murder rate.

Harvard economics professor Roland Fryer wrote a paper about this six years ago, in which he showed a direct connection between viral police killings and a reduction in police contacts in the cities in which they took place. In short, as scrutiny and criticism ramped up, officers got spooked about making a mistake and becoming front-page news. The results were record increases in murder in the Black community.

This phenomenon was most prominently displayed after George Floyd's death in 2020, when police officers were stereotyped across the country and the Black murder rate saw a 2,500-victim increase from the year before. Kaepernick wasn't single-handedly responsible for this, but he embodied the mentality that helped get a lot of people killed.

Again, another mark against Kaepernick's "peaceful" persona. Hysteria gripped the country in the spring of 2020, with 19 deaths occurring in the first two weeks of the Floyd "protests" along with billions of dollars’ worth of damage. Tweets such as this couldn't have helped.

"When civility leads to death, revolting is the only logical reaction," Kaepernick posted. "The cries for people will rain down, and when they do, they will land on deaf ears, because your violence has brought this resistance."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

I don't see a gentle soul simply trying to do what's right with a quote like that. I see someone who's lost his way. Regardless of Colin's initial intent, there's a strong argument that he made the country worse.

The way Kaepernick is hyped in certain circles, I wouldn't be surprised if there are throngs of people who think he was on top of his game when he was essentially ousted from the league. But the guy went 1-10 as a starter in his final year with the 49ers, when he completed less than 60 percent of his passes and posted a QBR of 49.2.

He wasn't a disaster— he threw 16 touchdowns against four interceptions — but he wasn't nearly good enough to offset the distraction he'd become. Kaepernick made a choice to kneel and upset millions of Americans — some of whom thought he was disrespecting the flag, and others who thought he was pushing a false narrative in regard to the frequency of police killings. But if he could sling it like Aaron Rodgers, Tom Brady or Drew Brees, he'd have found a roster.

Back in November of 2019, 25 NFL teams were expected to watch Kaepernick work out at the Falcons facility in Georgia. But three hours before said workout, he decided he wanted to change the location to a high school about 60 miles away without the blessing of the NFL. He claimed it was over an insufficient liability waiver.

The league — who Kaepernick had previously sued for millions — said the waiver was standard procedure. Who you believe is your call, but just like that, it seemed that the teams who were willing to take a look decided he wasn't worth the trouble.

Kaepernick had to know that he didn't have the leverage in that situation. But it's unlikely that he cared. The notoriety he gained as an activist (which helped land him a multi-million dollar Nike deal) seemed to be satisfying enough. No need for the grind of a 16-game season to disrupt that.

But the people interviewing Kaepernick aren't going to question his motives. They've seemed to have little interest in anything but fawning.

He took a knee — and everyone he talks to genuflects.

item.title: One of history's most famous sayings about Rome may be wrong, new study suggests
item.description: The Roman Empire's vast road network favored Constantinople as a key overland travel hub, a study says, yet experts argue Rome remained the true center of power.
item.content:encoded:
A sweeping new study of the Roman Empire's vast road network is challenging the age-old saying, "All roads lead to Rome."

The study, published Sept. 15 in the journal Nature Communications, analyzed roughly 190,000 miles of Roman roads spanning Europe, the Middle East and North Africa.

The team combined existing data to create a new map of the Roman Empire's road network and analyze its structure on an empire-wide scale.

CONSTRUCTION WORKERS CLEARING OLD BOMBS UNEXPECTEDLY FIND 'IMPORTANT' ANCIENT SANCTUARY

The study's lead researcher, Tom Brughmans, a classical archaeologist at Aarhus University in Denmark, and his colleagues found that Rome was not uniquely central to the empire's road network, with provincial capitals playing key roles in overland travel.

Constantinople, now known as Istanbul, Turkey, emerged as a far more central hub for overland travel after Emperor Constantine made it the imperial capital in the fourth century A.D.

Constantinople's location between Europe and Asia made it exceptionally central to travel across the empire, according to the researchers.

Therefore, the phrase "all roads lead to Rome" — coined centuries after the Roman Empire fell — may not reveal the whole story.

ANCIENT CLUE CRACKS OPEN A 2,000-YEAR-OLD MYSTERY NEAR FAMED COLOSSEUM

Brughmans told Fox News Digital that the proverb, which he described as medieval in origin, should not be taken literally — noting that none of the roads in Roman Britain actually led to Rome.

"It is quite surprising how persistently this maxim has shaped popular understanding of Roman roads," he said.

"It’s fair to say our study complicates the proverb," Brughmans added. "I prefer to say, ‘All roads lead to Rome and everywhere else.'"

RARE PAGAN MASTERPIECE EMERGES NEAR WHERE ST PAUL SPREAD TEACHINGS OF CHRISTIANITY

Taco Terpstra, a professor of history and classics at Northwestern University in Illinois, told Fox News Digital the findings don't diminish Rome's importance as the center of the empire — nor do the study's authors argue otherwise.

Terpstra, who was not involved in the research, noted that Constantinople "was only created as such in the fourth century."

"Before that, it was a sleepy fishing town called Byzantium," he said. "So, we have to be careful a little bit about what time period we’re looking at."

He added, "But once Constantinople becomes de facto the capital of the empire, it is clear that it attracts a lot of overland connectivity."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Rome did remain the center of political, military and ideological power for centuries, Terpstra said.

"Rome is the center of the empire. This is where power lies," he said, noting that the empire's second-largest city, Alexandria, dwarfed in comparison with roughly half Rome's population.

"This is where the emperor is. This is where the Senate is. ... [It was the] largest city in the empire, a million inhabitants."

The study also examined another hallmark of Roman engineering: the remarkable straightness of its roads, though difficult terrain often forced routes to deviate from a direct path.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

The roads were "about as straight as the Romans could make them" given the technology available at the time, Terpstra said.

The roads initially served a military purpose, the professor added. They allowed troops to move quickly through conquered territory before also taking on an important economic role.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"The roads in the first instance, and it’s often forgotten, were military infrastructure," he said. "These were in the first place, after the conquest, intended to move troops quickly."

And although Roman roads have stood the test of time and remain a marvel of ancient engineering, Terpstra said they were secondary to maritime transportation across the empire — which was far cheaper when it came to transporting goods.

"The main transportation network of the Roman Empire is maritime," he said. "That is really where the major connectivity lies."

item.title: Texas prosecutors take death penalty off the table for man accused of murdering wife and fleeing to Italy
item.description: Lee Gilley fled the United States to Italy using forged documents and a fake name after allegedly killing his pregnant wife in Harris County, Texas.
item.content:encoded:
Texas prosecutors announced they won't seek the death penalty against a man accused of killing his wife and fleeing the country as his trial was set to begin, they told an Italian court, clearing a path for his extradition to the United States.

Lee Gilley, 39, faces a capital murder charge in connection with the October 2024 death of his wife, Christa, who was nine weeks pregnant when she died. The Harris County Medical Examiner's office determined her death was a homicide resulting from neck compression. He pleaded not guilty.

Authorities allege Gilley removed his ankle monitor on May 1 and left Texas before his scheduled trial was to begin. He got to the Milan Malpensa Airport in Italy by using a fake name and forged travel documents, according to court records. He was taken into custody by Italian authorities.

EXCLUSIVE: FBI EXTRADITIONS SOAR AS PATEL RAMPS UP FOREIGN OUTREACH, VOWS 'NO SANCTUARY'

Gilley's American attorney, Dick DeGuerin, previously told Fox News Digital that Italy wanted a written guarantee prosecutors wouldn't seek the death penalty before considering his return. Italian authorities may also demand assurances against a sentence of life without parole, he said.

The Harris County District Attorney said in a Friday court filing obtained by Fox News Digital that it won't be pursuing the death penalty against Gilley, but stopped short of taking life without parole off the table as a possible sentence.

MULTIPLE DEATH SENTENCES IN DIFFERENT STATES ARE SET TO BE CARRIED OUT WITHIN 24 HOURS: 'NOT VERY COMMON'

READ THE FILING:

"Nevertheless, the State files this unusual notice because the defendant continues to falsely insist to the Court of Appeal of Turin that he remains subject to the death penalty, and that a judge or jury could assess the death penalty notwithstanding the State's decision not to seek that punishment," the filing states.

Harris County prosecutors also accused Gilley's Italian attorney, Monica Grosso, of misleading the Turin Court of Appeal by telling it that commutation is impossible for someone sentenced to life without parole.

CALIFORNIA SUED OVER POLICY THAT COULD FREE SERIAL KILLERS AS LACI PETERSON'S FRIEND SOUNDS ALARM

"Should he be sentenced to life without parole, the defendant would be eligible for commutation consideration," prosecutors said. "It is our hope that this notice will put an end to the defendant's charade so that he can be tried by a jury or judge in the United States and the victims receive the justice they deserve."

A hearing was held before the Turin Court of Appeal on Sept. 7. DeGuerin told Fox News Digital that Gilley's extradition was again delayed.

FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

During a July 15 hearing at the Turin Court of Appeal, Gilley said he is seeking protection in Italy, according to NBC News. The Turin Court of Appeal blocked the extradition request during a hearing on July 20.

Grosso also said the defense contends Christa had a blood disorder and that blood discovered in the couple's bedroom did not align with the prosecution's version of how she died.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

"I am seeking protection in Italy," Gilley said. "They want to punish me, and I am asking for protection for myself and my children."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

Anne Bremner, who advocated for Amanda Knox while she was detained in Italy, told Fox News Digital that Gilley made a "very smart choice" in fleeing to Italy, a country that doesn't have a death penalty.

SEND US A TIP

"It was a very smart choice for him to flee to Italy of all countries because they do not have the death penalty they bought extradite if a death penalty is on the table," Bremner said.

GOT A TIP?

Bremner said she thinks that prosecutors taking the death penalty off the table "would be enough for the Italians to allow him to come back to Texas," but said it's possible Italian courts may make more demands.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

Bremner said the outcome could set a troubling example for other defendants facing capital charges.

GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL

"There's potential for somebody to look at that and say, 'Well, I guess I could do that too and flee the death penalty that's on the table.' And the answer is yes, because obviously in this case, he jumped bail, had forged documents and made it all the way to Italy before he was caught," Bremner said. "And he's not going to face the death penalty, where it clearly was on the table, or should have been, under the law in Texas."

Gilley will have another hearing at the Turin Court of Appeal on Oct. 7.

item.title: Mississippi grand jury declines to indict anyone in death of 18-year-old who vanished in coastal waters
item.description: A 23-member Jackson County grand jury heard from 43 witnesses and found Nolan Wells' death on Horn Island was consistent with drowning, not foul play.
item.content:encoded:
A Mississippi grand jury found no evidence of criminal conduct in the death of 18-year-old Nolan Wells, concluding that the college football player’s body was found under circumstances "consistent with drowning" after his disappearance during a Fourth of July boating trip.

The 23-member Jackson County grand jury found no criminal charges were warranted after hearing from 43 witnesses and reviewing physical and digital evidence, police reports, interviews, videos, images and maps, according to the grand jury report released by District Attorney Angel Myers McIlrath on Monday.

Wells disappeared July 4 after traveling with friends to Horn Island, a barrier island off Mississippi’s Gulf Coast. His body was recovered in the waters off the island two days later after a multi-agency search.

NEW AUDIO RELEASED FOLLOWING NOLAN WELLS DISAPPEARANCE DOESN'T SHOW 'ANYTHING NEFARIOUS': RETIRED FBI AGENT

The report said the "position of, condition of, time of discovery, and location" of Wells’ body were consistent with drowning and that there was "no credible evidence" anyone traveling to or from the island committed a crime related to his death.

The grand jury also found that bruising on the back of Wells’ head was "not a fatal injury." The report said there was no evidence of a fatal injury or organic disease, though investigators could not determine how Wells suffered the bruise.

One witness testified that Wells was seen slipping "awkwardly off the side of a boat" around the time he was last seen. The witness could not say whether Wells struck his head during the fall and said Wells continued socializing afterward and did not appear injured.

The report also said Wells was not involved in a physical altercation or argument that day.

SHARPTON OFFERS $50K FOR NOLAN WELLS CASE ARREST WITH LAWYER TO RELEASE AUTOPSY AT NAACP

A private autopsy commissioned by Wells’ family had previously listed his cause and manner of death as "undetermined pending investigation."

During a July 22 news conference, civil rights attorney Ben Crump said the examination found an area of "red discoloration" on the back of Wells’ head, but pathologist Dr. Roger Mitchell could not determine a cause or manner of death.

Questions had also been raised about Wells’ alcohol consumption.

A July 5 Mississippi Department of Marine Resources Marine Patrol email previously obtained by Fox News Digital listed Wells’ alcohol intake as "heavy" while authorities searched for him. The email did not identify the source of that information.

The grand jury found that Wells bought alcohol using a fake ID and that no adults of legal drinking age provided him with alcohol on the island.

The report said toxicology testing was "not particularly informative" because decomposition fluid is an unreliable source for determining substance levels in a body. It also said there was no cocaine in Wells’ system and no evidence he had ever used the drug.

The report also shed light on Wells’ cellphone, which was taken back to the mainland without him.

CAJUN NAVY LEADER WARNS NOLAN WELLS' SEARCH AREA HAS DEADLY 'WASHING MACHINE' CURRENTS: 'LOTS OF DROWNINGS'

The grand jury said it was not unusual for people visiting the island to return on different boats or leave phones and other belongings aboard boats while socializing. Wells’ phone was not the only one that returned to the mainland without its owner, according to the report.

Wells’ death attracted national attention and widespread speculation online.

The grand jury said allegations targeting the occupants of the three boats involved in the trip had spread to their relatives and friends, calling the "public attacks" "malicious, false," and having "no truth in fact or evidence."

Wells’ family was given an opportunity to provide evidence from its private investigation. According to the report, the family’s attorneys said their investigation had found no witnesses or evidence they reasonably believed pointed to potential criminal activity that warranted referral.

The case could still return to a grand jury if new evidence emerges. Mississippi has no statute of limitations on homicide cases.

"If credible evidence comes to light in the future that suggests Mr. Wells’ death was non-accidental, this matter should be represented to the Jackson County Grand Jury for further consideration," the report said.

Fox News Digital's Stepheny Price contributed to this report.

item.title: Giants' Jaxson Dart tried to reenter game with knee injury but had jersey taken away: reports
item.description: Jaxson Dart reportedly tried to reenter the game after his knee injury, but the Giants went as far as taking his jersey to keep him sidelined.
item.content:encoded:
Jaxson Dart reportedly wanted to show just how much of a gamer he really is after going down with a knee injury in the first quarter of the New York Giants’ loss to the Los Angeles Rams on Monday.

The quarterback tried to reenter the game in the first half in spite of the knee issue but the team wouldn’t let him, ESPN reported. A separate ESPN report added that the Giants went as far as taking Dart’s jersey from him to prevent any inkling that he would be able to play.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Dart returned to the sideline in street clothes and a shiny chain around his neck.

Dart left the matchup seven snaps into the second game of the 2026 season when he was hit twice by Rams defenders on a throw to Theo Johnson. The second-year quarterback’s knee bent awkwardly and he was writhing in pain as trainers came out to look at him. He gingerly walked off the field and into the locker room under his own power.

The Giants would not confirm reports that Dart sprained his MCL.

"That's in the neighborhood of it, I would say," Giants coach John Harbaugh said. "We'll get an MRI (on Tuesday) and have a real good feel for it, and give you more information from there."

Taking the reports for what they’re worth, Dart showed more heart than what was shown on the field after he left the game. The team looked deflated from the second he went down grabbing his knee.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Jameis Winston did little to inspire that he could handle the reins in Dart’s absence. The defense, while making some plays and forcing turnovers on the Rams, allowed Matthew Stafford to throw four touchdown passes – two to Davante Adams, who had eight catches for 195 yards.

"Any time your quarterback goes down, obviously that's a gut punch to the team, right?" Winston said.

Harbaugh said the task at hand right now is to not "lament" the injuries as Malik Nabers and Brian Burns were among those banged up during the game.

The schedule may look cookie-cutter on paper – but it’s far from it based on the effort shown against the Rams. If Dart does miss at least four weeks, he will be out against the Tennessee Titans, Arizona Cardinals, Washington Commanders and New Orleans Saints.

All of those games are winnable but the team will really have to dig deep to pull itself out of a mental hole.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

item.title: Middle East takes center stage at UN as regional leaders confront Iran war, Gaza and Houthi threat
item.description: Gulf leaders arrive at the United Nations General Assembly facing urgent questions about Iran, Houthi threats and Gaza's future amid shifting alliances.
item.content:encoded:
UNITED NATIONS — The Middle East will take center stage when world leaders open the U.N. General Assembly's annual debate Tuesday, with some of Washington's most important regional partners arriving in New York facing a question: What will the region look like after months of war with Iran, renewed Houthi attacks and an uncertain future for Gaza?

Leaders from Jordan, Türkiye, Qatar and Egypt are expected to address the Assembly during the annual General Debate, which begins Sept. 22. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is also scheduled to attend.

President Donald Trump is expected to meet Gulf leaders on the sidelines of UNGA to discuss the Iran conflict and the region's future. U.S. Ambassador to the U.N. Mike Waltz told Fox News Digital that the administration wants to hear directly from Gulf leaders about their concerns, describing the meeting as an important opportunity for diplomacy.

TRUMP WELCOMES NETANYAHU TO WHITE HOUSE AS RAGING IRAN WAR THREATENS TO SOUR US-ISRAEL RELATIONSHIP

Rich Goldberg, a senior adviser at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, told Fox News Digital that the Iran war has fundamentally altered the region's strategic landscape, creating opportunities for new energy partnerships and closer cooperation between Israel and its Arab neighbors.

"The opportunity for regional integration and normalization works alongside energy infrastructure meeting the moment, the crisis of needing bypasses for Hormuz," Goldberg said.

He argued that a network of pipelines carrying Gulf energy overland to the Mediterranean, potentially through Israel, could reduce dependence on vulnerable shipping routes.

"We can make the Strait of Hormuz irrelevant," Goldberg said, describing potential energy links between Saudi Arabia and Israel, as well as routes connecting Qatar to the Mediterranean.

IRAN-BACKED TERROR GROUP’S LATEST TERRITORIAL GRAB THREATENS SECOND GLOBAL SHIPPING CHOKEPOINT

But the threat to regional energy supplies now extends beyond Hormuz. The Houthis' offensive along Yemen's Red Sea coast has raised new concerns over the Bab el-Mandeb, another critical maritime choke point. Washington Institute analysts April Longley Alley and Allison Minor wrote in a Sept. 11 analysis that the offensive had "shattered the status quo" along Yemen's western coast.

NETANYAHU REJECTS BOARD OF PEACE'S GAZA PLAN: NO 'WITHDRAWAL UNTIL HAMAS IS GENUINELY DISARMED'

Gaza presents a separate diplomatic challenge, with Arab governments seeking a political settlement while differing with Israel over Palestinian statehood and the territory's future.

In a Sept. 6 joint statement, the foreign ministers of Jordan, Egypt, Qatar, Türkiye, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Indonesia and Pakistan rejected proposals to forcibly displace Palestinians from Gaza and reiterated support for a Palestinian state along the 1967 lines, with East Jerusalem as its capital. They also warned that displacement proposals risk undermining Trump's Gaza peace plan.

ISRAEL’S E1 PLAN EXPLAINED: THE JERUSALEM-AREA CORRIDOR SPARKING INTERNATIONAL BACKLASH

Qatar has simultaneously condemned renewed Iranian attacks against Arab states and Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and Red Sea shipping, while insisting that the Palestinian issue remains a priority.

In a Sept. 8 joint statement, the leaders of France, Britain and Canada announced plans to ban imports from Israeli settlements and pursue targeted measures against settlements and those who facilitate them. They also said they would co-chair a meeting during UNGA to advance a two-state solution, one year after recognizing Palestinian statehood.

The diplomatic divisions will also be reflected in who can address the U.N. in person. Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas was denied a U.S. visa for the second consecutive year. The General Assembly voted Thursday to allow him to deliver his address by video.

Netanyahu, meanwhile, is expected to travel to New York weeks before Israel's Oct. 27 parliamentary elections, the country's first national vote since the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attacks, amid declining international support for Israel. A June 2026 Pew Research Center survey found that a median of 67% of adults across 36 countries held unfavorable views of Israel, compared with 25% who viewed it favorably.

For Washington, the challenge is balancing its regional security relationships with competing demands over Gaza and the future of relations with Israel.

TRUMP CALLS ON ARAB NATIONS TO SIGN ABRAHAM ACCORDS

Goldberg predicted that some of the most consequential discussions would take place away from the General Assembly podium, with Arab leaders delivering one message publicly and another in private meetings with Trump and senior U.S. officials.

"We may see the old propaganda of criticizing Israel and saying everybody wants a different future, and they're going to support Gaza and the Palestinians, they demand a Palestinian state," Goldberg said.

Behind closed doors, he predicted the discussions would focus on U.S. security guarantees, the next steps in confronting Iran and expanding regional energy infrastructure.

"What will be a pathway forward politically that the U.S. can provide to these leaders so that they can normalize with Israel alongside the necessary infrastructure upgrades that they need to make for their own energy securities and physical securities going forward?" Goldberg said.

item.title: Trump warns he'll be 'last Republican president' if Senate GOP doesn't make major change
item.description: Donald Trump warns he could be the last Republican president if the Senate filibuster survives, citing D.C. and Puerto Rico statehood threats.
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump has changed his pitch to wary Republicans who are hesitant to undo a decades-old safeguard in the Senate: if they do nothing, he may be the last Republican president.

Trump has long demanded that Republicans nuke the filibuster, which has blocked key parts of his agenda, to pass the SAVE America Act. He has warned that Democrats would eliminate the firewall themselves if they regain power, allowing them to push through their most partisan priorities.

Now, he’s warning that if Republicans don’t pull the trigger, Washington, D.C., and Puerto Rico will become states and elect only Democrats to Congress, likely foiling the chances of a future Republican winning the White House.

DEM INSURGENT TURNS ON THE CHARM WITH PARTY ESTABLISHMENT AS SCHUMER LEAVES BITTER FEUD HANGING

"If Senate Republicans don't TERMINATE THE FILIBUSTER, the Dumocrats will, and I will be, despite how well our Party is doing, the last Republican President," Trump said on Truth Social.

"The Dumocrats will vote in Puerto Rico (4% Republican Vote), and Washington, D.C. (3% Republican Vote), pick up 4 Senators, 8 Congressmen/women, tremendous numbers of Popular and Electoral College Votes and, importantly, control the Voting Mechanisms and Systems, both Legal and otherwise, throughout the United States," he continued.

"It will be impossible for Republicans to ever win an Election again. In other words, it will be THE END OF AMERICA! Thank you for your attention to this matter."

REPUBLICAN SOUNDS ALARM ON RISING DEM STAR: 'THIS GUY’S GOING TO BE A PROBLEM'

Voters in Washington, D.C., which carries three electoral votes, can vote in both presidential primaries and in the general election thanks to the 23rd Amendment. Those contests tend to heavily skew in favor of Democratic candidates.

Voters in Puerto Rico can also participate in presidential primaries, but not federal elections. And given that neither is a state, they don’t have true representation in Congress — Puerto Rico and Washington have non-voting delegates in the House, and the district has a shadow senator in the upper chamber.

Democrats have shown a desire to make both states, pushing legislation in 2023 to do so.

Meanwhile, the Senate filibuster is the 60-vote threshold that applies to most bills in the upper chamber, and given the nature of the thin majorities that either party has commanded in recent years, that means legislation typically has to be bipartisan to advance.

TRUMP DEMANDS THUNE KEEP SENATE IN SESSION UNTIL SAVE AMERICA ACT PASSES

Because of that, some of Trump’s agenda has been stonewalled. Most notably, the SAVE America Act has withered on the vine as Democrats, joined by a handful of Republicans, have continued to block the bill on the floor.

The last time the filibuster was put to the test was when Democrats controlled the Senate in 2022. Schumer, who was majority leader at the time, tried to change the rules for a "talking filibuster" to pass voting rights legislation.

But it’s a pitch that is going nowhere fast with Republicans, who have dug in their heels against terminating the filibuster throughout Trump’s second term.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., has time and again pushed back on the demand, arguing that the GOP doesn’t have the votes to kill the filibuster.

Thune earlier this month told the Ruthless Podcast that at least half of the Senate GOP support keeping the filibuster in place.

"At some point, Democrats may try and steal the car, but we’re not going to hand them the keys," Thune said.

"We would enable all the crazy stuff they would do, whether it’s adding Puerto Rico and D.C. as states, whether it’s federalizing elections, or packing the Supreme Court," he continued.

item.title: Man challenging 150-year-old ban on making liquor at home hopes Supreme Court takes his case
item.description: An Ohio man's Supreme Court case challenges a more than 150-year federal ban on home distilling that carries felony charges, fines and up to five years in prison.
item.content:encoded:
Americans can brew beer in their kitchens and make wine at home, but just try making a bottle of whiskey or gin — and people can run afoul of a federal law that dates back more than 150 years.

That distinction caught the attention of Ohio resident John Ream, a former aerospace engineer and home-brewing enthusiast who wants to distill small quantities of spirits at home for himself and his wife.

"It is perfectly legal to make beer at home or to make wine at home, but if you make even a single ounce of distilled spirits at home, it is a federal felony," Robert Alt, an attorney representing Ream, told Fox News Digital.

GEORGE WASHINGTON'S 1757 BEER RECIPE BROUGHT BACK TO LIFE AHEAD OF AMERICA'S 250TH BIRTHDAY

Ream's interest in making his own drinks began when his then-fiancée, now wife, Kristin, gave him a home-brewing kit.

"Brewing was the perfect combination of art and science, and my engineering brain just totally latched onto it," Ream told the Buckeye Institute, an Ohio-based think tank where Alt serves as president and CEO.

After years of experimenting with brewing, Ream and his wife opened Trek Brewing Company in Newark, Ohio.

But when Ream became interested in experimenting with distilled spirits at home, he encountered a very different set of rules.

'GOD BLESS THE USA' STAR REVIVES PATRIOTIC SPIRIT BRAND BENEFITING VETERANS FOR AMERICA'S 250TH BIRTHDAY

Federal law allows qualifying home production of beer and wine for personal or family use — but distilled spirits cannot legally be produced at home. Federal violations can carry significant fines and prison time.

The debate has also attracted attention within the home-brewing community. 

The American Homebrewers Association, a trade group based in Boulder, Colorado, said this year that it does not have an official position on legalizing home distilling. It noted that some of its members distill at home and emphasized education and safety around beverage-making hobbies.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Why federal law treats distilled spirits differently from beer and wine has roots stretching back more than two centuries.

The federal government began taxing distilled spirits in 1791, a levy that helped spark the Whiskey Rebellion several years later, according to the National Archives. 

In 1868, amid concerns about tax evasion and the collection of liquor taxes, Congress enacted a broader system regulating distilled spirits that included restrictions on where distilleries could operate.

More than 150 years later, that old tax fight has produced a modern question.

"To what extent can Congress regulate local non-commercial otherwise lawful [activity] that you engage in, in your very home?" Alt said. 

"That really is the core question in this case."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Two federal appeals courts have given different answers to the constitutional question behind that debate.

The Sixth Circuit ruled against Ream in April, concluding that the home-distilling restriction could lawfully be used to support the collection of federal liquor taxes.

But 11 days earlier, the Fifth Circuit reached the opposite conclusion in a separate challenge, ruling that Congress' taxing authority did not justify the restriction.

Both disputes have reached the Supreme Court, though the justices have not agreed to hear either case.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"The Supreme Court gets a lot of petitions for review every year, between 7,000 and 10,000," Alt said. "And the court, at this point, only hears about 60 cases."

The federal government argues that the restriction remains a permissible part of the system used to protect and collect federal excise taxes on distilled spirits.

Ream and other home-distilling advocates contend that collecting those taxes does not give Congress the authority to prohibit the hobby altogether.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

For home brewers interested in taking the next step from beer or wine to whiskey, gin or other spirits, the dispute could ultimately determine whether a hobby long prohibited under federal law can move out of the commercial distillery and into the home.

"This would be a wonderful opportunity to raise a glass to freedom and to limited government," Alt said.

Fox News Digital's Deirdre Bardolf contributed to this report.

item.title: From the Chargers to the Colts and Falcons, which of the NFL's eight winless teams are already in panic mode
item.description: Eight NFL teams, including the Colts and Chargers, sit at 0-2, and history says only one of the eight will probably make the postseason so who's panicking
item.content:encoded:
We are only two games into the NFL season and already multiple teams need to be in full-on panic alert.

That's because the season offers only 17 games and losing the first two is, well, a major problem. Forty teams have started a season 0-2 since 2021 when the league went to a 17-game schedule.

Of those 40 teams, only eight rallied to make the playoffs. That means 20% of the teams starting 0-2 since 2021 made the postseason.

And 80% did not.

COMMANDERS FACE CRITICAL DECISION ON JAYDEN DANIELS' ELBOW AS SPECIALISTS REVIEW MRI RESULTS

If the math holds, that means maybe only one of the eight teams that started the season with a 0-2 record will make it to the postseason.

So, yeah, fanbases are panicking. Pundits invested in their opinions looking good are panicking.

And teams are trying to resist the urge to panic.

But which of the NFL's eight winless teams legitimately should panic? Here are the answers:

Los Angeles Chargers: Definitely time to panic. John Harbaugh has never been 0-2 in his life and there is nothing that suggests he knows how to handle the crisis. He handed the reins of the offense to new offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel, who is busy ruining quarterback Justin Herbert. McDaniel flipped Herbert's shotgun stance, gave him an offense built to have Tyreek Hill and Jaylen Waddle but lacks both, and isn't known for making adjustments. Oh, yeah, check out the killer schedule for the next seven games.

Houston Texans: Not time to panic yet because this team under coach DeMeco Ryans has been a notoriously slow starter. They started 0-2 in 2023 and again last season, and made the playoffs both seasons. But this year they've lost two home games to open the season, and another loss will have fans and media in Houston losing their minds. The offensive line is a problem, there is no dynamic playmaker at running back, and the defense which finished second in points allowed last season is currently ranked 25th.

Indianapolis Colts: Head coach Shane Steichen and general manager Chris Ballard must win or they'll be fired. Problem is, the Colts have lost nine consecutive games dating back to last season. Cornerback Sauce Gardner, who joined the team last November in a blockbuster trade that sent two first-round picks and a player to the New York Jets, has not won a game with the Colts in the United States. Another loss Sunday, coincidentally against the Texans, will make this a serious panic situation because jobs are at stake.

Miami Dolphins: No panic here. The Dolphins are a borderline Triple-A team and ownership, the personnel department and the coaching staff pretty much knew this before the season because that's how they authored it. It's one reason coach Jeff Hafley actually said, "success is not gonna be measured in wins and losses." The Dolphins are on a March to Arch (Manning) and they're right on course.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Tennessee Titans: It's not correct to say they're panicking because it's a first-year coaching staff and quarterback Cam Ward is only in his second NFL season. But owner Amy Adams Strunk in recent years has not blinked at getting rid of a couple of highly touted QBs while they were still on their rookie contracts, and a coach who lasted less than two seasons. This is not a stable or patient franchise, so panic is not far off barring a change of direction.

Washington Commanders: This is a desperate team. They have not only lost games but lost starting quarterback Jayden Daniels to a dislocated elbow. He may need surgery, which would end his season and effectively dash the team's postseason hopes. The Commanders badly need good news on the Daniels front because panic is this close to setting in.

BAKER MAYFIELD LOSES BET TO COACH TODD BOWLES, HAS 'ROUGH COUPLE OF DAYS' INCLUDING AT PRESS CONFERENCE

Tampa Bay Buccaneers: Todd Bowles wouldn't have panicked if he'd woken up in a flooded stateroom on the Titanic. But quarterback Baker Mayfield isn't wired like that. He's passionate, sensitive, and often led by raw emotion. So the danger of panic is real for a player pressing after getting a big contract and, so far, not living up to the bigger bucks.

Atlanta Falcons: They're not panicking yet because Michael Penix Jr. will start his first game of the season on Thursday. Any team getting its presumptive starting quarterback back in the lineup for the first time is actually upbeat rather than panicking. But Penix Jr. better perform, and the results must change.

item.title: El-Sayed’s Jewish outreach ignites ‘tokenism’ fury as Michigan GOP chair makes bold prediction
item.description: Roughly 500 Jewish Democrats signed an open letter backing Mike Rogers and denouncing Abdul El-Sayed's alleged ties to anti-Jewish elements.
item.content:encoded:
As some prominent Jewish Democrats in Michigan throw their support behind Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers, the state’s GOP chair told Fox News Digital he is confident that opposition to Abdul El-Sayed will spark a significant Jewish defection from the Democratic Party on Election Day.

"The big issue is Democratic donors who are Jewish, and what we’re hearing most of the angst is about from them, is El-Sayed," Michigan GOP Chairman Jim Runestad told Fox News Digital. "His off-the-charts comments and his associations are actually striking fear into the Jewish community here in the state of Michigan."

Indeed, roughly 500 individuals identifying as Jewish Democrats or independents living in Michigan have signed an open letter calling Rogers a "friend to the Jewish community" and warning that an El-Sayed victory could allow "far-left and anti-Jewish elements" to become dominant within the Democratic Party.

JEWISH DEMOCRATS ABANDON EL-SAYED FOR GOP RIVAL IN ALL-IMPORTANT BATTLEGROUND STATE

Amid his allegedly faltering Jewish support, El-Sayed released a video on social media where he showed himself spending Rosh Hashanah, essentially the Jewish New Year, with two Jewish women. The two women’s pro-Palestinian activism, along with criticism of their apparent unfamiliarity with the Hebrew prayers featured in the video, drew scrutiny from critics — including one Democratic state lawmaker.

"Man I really hate tokenism," Democrat state Rep. Noah Arbit, who represents the heavily Jewish town of West Bloomfield, wrote.

EL-SAYED TRIES TO MAKE PEACE WITH JEWISH DEMOCRATS BUT DRAWS LINE AT DUMPING HASAN PIKER

"This isn’t designed to appeal to the Jewish community. It’s for any non-Jews concerned about his bigotry who won’t immediately be suspicious," Jonathan Greenberg, a rabbi who leads the effort to combat antisemitism at a conservative advocacy group, wrote.

El-Sayed’s video nonetheless drew significant engagement on social media, generating thousands of interactions across X and TikTok.

Even if El-Sayed alienates Jewish voters, it is unclear if that will have lasting, or even down-ballot, effects for Democrats in Michigan. The open letter endorsing Rogers, for instance, makes clear that signatories do not necessarily support President Donald Trump and states that their support is specific to "this year and in this Senate race."

As it relates to the short term, the Rogers campaign claims that their Jewish outreach efforts have been successful.

JEWISH DEM DEFECTIONS THREATEN EL-SAYED IN MICHIGAN SENATE RACE DECIDED BY RAZOR-THIN MARGINS

A source within the Rogers campaign told Fox News Digital that their social media inboxes are "constantly" being filled with positive messages from Jewish voters and that they’ve been "inundated" with outreach more generally. The source also claimed that the fundraisers they held with donors have gone well, though they did not provide specific numbers.

Runestad, however, is confident that Republicans can make lasting gains with the Jewish community if they play their cards right.

"We think there’s also an opening for Republicans long term to start getting the Jewish community to look at the Republicans from a different perspective," he told Fox News Digital. "We have been very connected to so much of what the Jewish community believes in terms of being entrepreneurial, supporting lower taxes and reducing regulation."

While Jewish voters swinging significantly toward Rogers could benefit the Republican, he will also have to contend with El-Sayed’s strong support in Michigan’s Arab American community, particularly in Dearborn and Dearborn Heights, where he built a commanding advantage in the Democratic primary.

EX-HILLARY CLINTON STAFFER WARNS DEMOCRATS THAT COURTING FAR-LEFT COULD COST THEM JEWISH VOTERS

"We have been outreaching to the Jewish community here in Oakland County, which is a very substantial community, and I think we’re going to see a real sea change this cycle," Runestad said.

"The real concern for the Jewish community is someone like Hasan Piker. Anybody who has looked at his comments — they’re off the charts," he added. "This is like the right-hand man of El-Sayed, and some of his despicable antisemitic comments are certainly going to be brought to bear in this election. The Jewish community is becoming more and more aware of just how dangerous someone like Hasan Piker is and his connection to El-Sayed."

El-Sayed has dismissed his proximity to Piker as insignificant to Michigan voters and called the streamer’s assertion that America "deserved" 9/11 "dumb." He has also pushed back against claims that his campaign is floundering among Jewish voters.

"Abdul is grateful for the good conversations he’s had with Jewish leaders across Michigan, and he’ll continue to be actively engaged with communities to build the coalition that will defeat Rogers, restore Democratic control of the U.S. Senate, and put a much-needed check on Trump’s reckless agenda," campaign spokesman Cole Wozniak told Fox News Digital.

In response to the pro-Rogers open letter, liberal Jewish leaders in Michigan have collected signatures from over 800 people identifying as Jewish Michiganders affirming their support for El-Sayed, though noting that some of them disagree with him on foreign policy and other issues. El-Sayed has made assuaging the concerns of Michigan Jews a priority for his campaign, courting endorsements from high-profile Jewish lawmakers and meeting frequently with members of the community.

item.title: Anxiety grows over emerging election issue, but GOP says Washington isn't the answer
item.description: Sen. Jon Husted and Mike Rogers say data center decisions should stay local, not federal, as 70% of Americans oppose new AI facilities nearby.
item.content:encoded:
Public perception is everything heading into a crucial midterm election fight, and voters across the political spectrum have laid down the gauntlet over their view of data centers this cycle.

Republicans running for power in the Senate are keenly aware that their voters aren’t happy about data centers, according to recent polling. While they believe that the construction of the windowless, hulking behemoths should be slowed or halted, they don’t want the federal government to play an outsized role.

"The data center companies haven't done a very good job of explaining why they should be allowed to develop in communities," Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, told Fox News Digital at the GOP’s midterm convention in Dallas.

HAWLEY TAKES AIM AT 'CORPORATE WELFARE' AFTER GOP-BACKED TAX BREAK BOOSTED CONTROVERSIAL INDUSTRY

"But the bottom line is, that should be a local decision, not a federal decision," he continued. "I don't want the federal government telling you that you must have a data center or that you can't have a data center. That's a local decision. Some people will say yes, some people will no."

A Gallup Poll published in May found that 70% of Americans don’t want new data centers for artificial intelligence (AI) constructed in their towns and cities. Many of their concerns are about the impact that a new data center could have on their bills, be it through spikes in water or electricity costs.

Husted is one of a handful of vulnerable Republicans running in this cycle, and he, like others, is hearing about data centers and their impact routinely on the campaign trail.

He attempted to pass a bill quickly on the Senate floor last week that would have tried to tackle the latter issue of booming electricity costs by preventing AI and tech companies from placing the burden of power grid infrastructure upgrades on taxpayers, but was blocked by Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., despite the bill having passed the House 417 to 3.

AI'S MASSIVE APPETITE FOR POWER, WATER IGNITES FIGHT IN HIGH-STAKES TEXAS SENATE RACE

"Rather than voluntary pledges, or suggestions to states, Congress needs to pass real legislation with real teeth," Heinrich said.

item.title: Trump’s Greenland deal set for signing after monthslong fight over US control
item.description: Trump, Denmark and Greenland will sign a historic Arctic security agreement at the U.N., granting the U.S. permanent military rights on the island.
item.content:encoded:
The U.S., Denmark and Greenland are set to formally sign President Trump’s new Greenland security agreement on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly Tuesday, cementing permanent U.S. military rights on the strategically vital Arctic island after months of negotiations over Trump’s push for greater American control.

Trump, Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of Denmark and Prime Minister Jens-Frederick Nielsen of Greenland will meet Tuesday morning for a trilateral signing ceremony, a White House official told Fox News Digital.

The U.S. has held extensive military rights in Greenland for decades under a 1951 defense agreement, but administration officials say the new pact goes further by allowing Washington to establish additional military installations without separate Danish or Greenlandic approval, explicitly barring adversaries from establishing a military presence and creating a mechanism to block adversarial investment in sensitive sectors.

TRUMP DECLARES VICTORY IN HISTORIC DEAL WITH GREENLAND AS HE SECURES 'PERMANENT' US MILITARY RIGHTS

The agreement stops short of the territorial acquisition Trump had sought for much of the year, when he repeatedly argued that U.S. ownership of Greenland was necessary for national security and pressed Denmark to relinquish control of the strategically located Arctic territory.

Those demands sparked a diplomatic standoff with Copenhagen and Nuuk, where leaders insisted Greenland was not for sale and stressed that its future could be decided only by the Greenlandic people.

DENMARK VOWS TO DEFEND GREENLAND AFTER TRUMP REITERATES US SHOULD CONTROL TERRITORY

Greenland is a self-governing territory within the Kingdom of Denmark, with Copenhagen retaining authority over foreign, defense and security policy while Greenland controls many of its domestic affairs, including mineral resources.

The new agreement instead leaves sovereignty unchanged while granting Washington expanded and permanent security rights. Frederiksen has emphasized that the pact recognizes "the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom" as well as Greenlanders’ right to self-determination, even as Trump has characterized the agreement as giving the U.S. "permanent control" over Greenland’s security.

For Greenland, Tuesday’s signing is also intended to close a turbulent chapter that left residents of the sparsely populated island wondering how far Trump was prepared to go to bring it under U.S. control.

Greenland Foreign Minister Múte B. Egede said the agreement respects the government’s longstanding "red lines," including Greenlanders’ right to self-determination, while allowing Nuuk to deepen defense cooperation with the United States and other Western allies. But he acknowledged that Trump’s earlier threats had taken a toll.

"The last nearly two years have been challenging for the Greenlandic population," Egede told Greenlandic broadcaster KNR. "Many people have been uncertain. Uncertain about our future."

Some Greenlanders remain wary as they wait to see the full agreement. Residents interviewed over the weekend expressed concern about how a larger American military footprint could affect life on the island, while Greenlandic politicians have urged the public to reserve judgment until the final text is signed and released.

Frederiksen, meanwhile, sought Monday to draw a firm line between expanded U.S. military access and American sovereignty over the territory.

"We are not giving up sovereignty," Frederiksen told Danish media in New York. "You can retain sovereignty and strengthen cooperation with other countries."

For the Trump administration, however, the agreement is fundamentally a national security deal — one official argues locks in U.S. access to a strategically vital piece of the Arctic regardless of how Greenland’s political status evolves in the decades ahead.

"This historic deal is a huge win for the United States and the American people," Secretary of State Marco Rubio told Fox News Digital when the agreement was announced Friday. "Thanks to President Trump’s vision and leadership, this historic agreement permanently guarantees U.S. security interests in the Arctic at zero cost to the U.S. taxpayer."

The "zero cost" refers to the United States making no payment to Denmark or Greenland in exchange for the new rights, a U.S. official told Fox News Digital. Any future construction of military installations or deployment of additional weapons and forces would still carry the normal costs associated with expanding the U.S. military presence.

The administration sees Greenland’s location as increasingly important as Russia and China compete for influence in the Arctic and advances in long-range missiles place greater importance on the northern approaches to the continental United States.

Greenland already hosts Pituffik Space Base, the northernmost U.S. military installation, which plays a key role in missile warning, missile defense and space surveillance. Administration officials say the new agreement would allow the U.S. to expand beyond its existing footprint and establish additional military installations when needed.

The expanded access could eventually support Trump’s planned Golden Dome missile defense system, according to a U.S. official involved in the negotiations.

The administration also sought guarantees aimed at preventing China, Russia or other potential adversaries from establishing their own foothold on the island. Under the agreement, non-NATO countries would be barred from establishing military bases or maintaining troops in Greenland.

"Greenland will forever be part of the strategic defense area of North America and exclude any adversary from it and the surrounding area," Rubio told Fox News Digital. "This deal permanently and completely addresses our national security concerns in Greenland."

Those restrictions extend beyond military installations. The agreement creates a process for blocking adversarial investments in sectors the U.S. considers particularly sensitive, including telecommunications infrastructure, undersea cables, ports and critical minerals.

U.S. officials have compared the effort to Washington’s concerns over the Panama Canal, where the Trump administration has sought to reduce Chinese involvement in strategically important infrastructure that officials warn could have potential dual military and commercial uses.

The administration argues that locking those restrictions into the Greenland agreement now will prevent a similar vulnerability from developing in the Arctic.
